CALIFORNIA INVASION OF PRIVACY ACT (CIPA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND OVERVIEW
This document states what California's Invasion of Privacy Act, Penal Code §§ 630-638.55 ("the Act"), provides regarding the recording, interception, and disclosure of communications. The Act is a distinct body of law from the workplace-monitoring principles addressed elsewhere in this corpus, which concern an employer's own computer, email, and network systems; the Act instead governs the recording, wiretapping, and interception of communications more broadly -- including telephone calls and in-person conversations -- regardless of whether an employment relationship is involved, and it carries both criminal penalties and a private civil right of action. This document states the Act's text and structure; it does not identify what law governs any particular recording, call, or conversation, and it does not state whether any specific practice of Acme, Inc. complies with the Act.

WIRETAPPING AND UNAUTHORIZED CONNECTION TO COMMUNICATION LINES
Penal Code § 631(a) separately prohibits two kinds of conduct. First, it prohibits intentionally tapping, or making any unauthorized connection -- whether physical, electrical, acoustic, inductive, or otherwise -- with any telegraph or telephone wire, line, cable, or instrument, including the wire, line, cable, or instrument of an internal telephonic communication system. Second, and separately, it prohibits willfully and without the consent of all parties to the communication, or in any other unauthorized manner, reading or attempting to read, or learning the contents or meaning of, a message, report, or communication while it is in transit or while it is being sent from, or received at, a place within California. Section 631(a) further prohibits using, or attempting to use, information obtained through either of those acts, and prohibits aiding, agreeing with, employing, or conspiring with another person to do any act the section describes. A violation is punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,500, by imprisonment in county jail not exceeding one year, by imprisonment under Penal Code § 1170(h), or by both a fine and imprisonment; a person previously convicted of violating § 631 or §§ 632, 632.5, 632.6, 632.7, or 636 faces an enhanced fine not exceeding $10,000, within the same range of imprisonment. Section 631(b) exempts public utilities and telephone companies (and their officers, employees, and agents) acting for the construction, maintenance, or operation of communications services and facilities, the use of equipment furnished under a public utility's tariffs, and telephonic communication systems used exclusively within a state or local correctional facility.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "intentionally taps, or makes any unauthorized connection, whether physically, electrically, acoustically, inductively, or otherwise, with any telegraph or telephone wire, line, cable, or instrument"
  — Cal. Penal Code § 631(a), Cal. Penal Code § 631(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=631.)
  "willfully and without the consent of all parties to the communication, or in any unauthorized manner, reads, or attempts to read, or to learn the contents or meaning of any message, report, or communication while the same is in transit"
  — Cal. Penal Code § 631(a), Cal. Penal Code § 631(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=631.)
  "is punishable by a fine not exceeding two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500), or by imprisonment in the county jail not exceeding one year, or by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170, or by both a fine and imprisonment in the county jail or pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 631(a), Cal. Penal Code § 631(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=631.)
  Known gap: The two prohibited-conduct quotes and the penalty quote below are all drawn from a single subdivision, § 631(a), of a single statutory section; they are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate § 631(b)'s exemptions in the statute's own full defined-term detail (e.g., its cross-reference to the "telephone company" definition in § 638(c)(3)), and it does not address how § 631 has been applied to non-telephonic technologies such as VoIP, text messaging, or internet-based communications -- that was not researched here.

RECORDING OR EAVESDROPPING ON A CONFIDENTIAL COMMUNICATION -- CONSENT OF ALL PARTIES
Penal Code § 632(a) prohibits a person from intentionally, and without the consent of all parties to a confidential communication, using an electronic amplifying or recording device to eavesdrop upon or record that confidential communication -- whether the communication is carried on in the parties' presence or by telegraph, telephone, or other device, with an exception for radio. This is the source of what is commonly called California's "all-party" or "two-party" consent rule: § 632(a)'s own text conditions the prohibition on the consent of all parties to the confidential communication, not merely one of them, which is a stricter consent requirement than the one-party-consent standard used under federal wiretap law and in a number of other states. A first violation is punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,500 per violation, by imprisonment in county jail not exceeding one year or in state prison, or by both; a person previously convicted of violating § 632 or §§ 631, 632.5, 632.6, 632.7, or 636 faces an enhanced fine not exceeding $10,000 per violation, within the same range of imprisonment. Section 632(e) exempts public utilities (and their officers, employees, and agents) acting for the construction, maintenance, or operation of communications services and facilities, the use of equipment furnished under a public utility's tariffs, and telephonic communication systems used exclusively within a state or local correctional facility; § 632(f) separately exempts the use of hearing aids and similar devices by persons with impaired hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A person who, intentionally and without the consent of all parties to a confidential communication, uses an electronic amplifying or recording device to eavesdrop upon or record the confidential communication, whether the communication is carried on among the parties in the presence of one another or by means of a telegraph, telephone, or other device, except a radio, shall be punished by a fine not exceeding two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per violation, or imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or in the state prison, or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 632(a), Cal. Penal Code § 632(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.)
  "If the person has previously been convicted of a violation of this section or Section 631, 632.5, 632.6, 632.7, or 636, the person shall be punished by a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per violation, by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or in the state prison, or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 632(a), Cal. Penal Code § 632(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.)
  Known gap: The core-prohibition quote and the repeat-offender penalty quote below are both drawn from a single subdivision, § 632(a), of a single statutory section; they are not independent of one another. This clause states § 632(a)'s all-party consent requirement as the statute's own text frames it; it does not address how courts have applied that requirement to specific recording methods or technologies (e.g., automated call-recording announcements, single-party recording apps, or out-of-state calls into California), which was not researched here.

"CONFIDENTIAL COMMUNICATION" AND "PERSON" DEFINED
Penal Code § 632(c) defines "confidential communication," for purposes of § 632, as any communication carried on in circumstances that may reasonably indicate that a party to it desires the communication to be confined to the parties to it. The definition expressly excludes a communication made in a public gathering, a communication made in any legislative, judicial, executive, or administrative proceeding open to the public, and any other circumstance in which the parties to the communication may reasonably expect that it may be overheard or recorded. Section 632(b) defines "person," for purposes of § 632, broadly to include an individual, business association, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or other legal entity, and an individual acting or purporting to act for or on behalf of a federal, state, or local government or subdivision of one -- but excludes an individual who is known by all parties to a confidential communication to be overhearing or recording it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“confidential communication” means any communication carried on in circumstances as may reasonably indicate that any party to the communication desires it to be confined to the parties thereto, but excludes a communication made in a public gathering or in any legislative, judicial, executive, or administrative proceeding open to the public, or in any other circumstance in which the parties to the communication may reasonably expect that the communication may be overheard or recorded."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 632(c), Cal. Penal Code § 632(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.)
  "excludes an individual known by all parties to a confidential communication to be overhearing or recording the communication."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 632(b), Cal. Penal Code § 632(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.)
  Known gap: The "confidential communication" definition and the "person" definition quoted below are both drawn from subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 632(b)-(c); they are not independent of one another. This clause states only § 632's own definitions; it does not restate case law applying those definitions to particular fact patterns (for example, what circumstances make an expectation of being overheard "reasonable"), which was not researched here.

EXCLUSION OF UNLAWFULLY OBTAINED EVIDENCE
Both § 631 and § 632 state their own evidentiary exclusion rule. Penal Code § 631(d) provides that, except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of § 631 itself, no evidence obtained in violation of § 631 is admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding. Penal Code § 632(d) states a parallel rule for § 632: except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of § 632, evidence obtained as a result of eavesdropping upon or recording a confidential communication in violation of § 632 is not admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of this section, no evidence obtained in violation of this section shall be admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 631(d), Cal. Penal Code § 631(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=631.)
  "Except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of this section, evidence obtained as a result of eavesdropping upon or recording a confidential communication in violation of this section is not admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 632(d), Cal. Penal Code § 632(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=632.)
  Known gap: Penal Code §§ 631 and 632 are separate, independently-numbered statutory sections, each stating its own exclusionary rule in its own subdivision (d); the two citations below are therefore independent of one another, not two subsections of a single section. This clause states only the Act's own admissibility rule; it does not address inadmissibility doctrines arising from other bodies of law -- such as the Evidence Code, or state or federal constitutional exclusionary rules -- which were not researched here.

PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION, STATUTORY DAMAGES, AND INJUNCTIVE RELIEF
Penal Code § 637.2(a) creates a private civil right of action: any person injured by a violation of "this chapter" -- Penal Code Chapter 1.5, Invasion of Privacy, §§ 630-638.55, which includes §§ 631 and 632 among its other sections -- may bring an action against the person who committed the violation for the greater of two amounts: $5,000 per violation, or three times the plaintiff's actual damages, if any. Section 637.2(b) separately authorizes an action, brought in accordance with the injunction provisions commencing at Code of Civil Procedure § 525, to enjoin and restrain a violation of the chapter, and allows a plaintiff to seek that injunctive relief and the damages described in § 637.2(a) in the same action. Section 637.2(c) states that suffering, or being threatened with, actual damages is not a necessary prerequisite to bringing an action under § 637.2.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any person who has been injured by a violation of this chapter may bring an action against the person who committed the violation for the greater of the following amounts: (1) Five thousand dollars ($5,000) per violation. (2) Three times the amount of actual damages, if any, sustained by the plaintiff."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(a), Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=637.2.)
  "Any person may, in accordance with Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, bring an action to enjoin and restrain any violation of this chapter, and may in the same action seek damages as provided by subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(b), Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=637.2.)
  "It is not a necessary prerequisite to an action pursuant to this section that the plaintiff has suffered, or be threatened with, actual damages."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(c), Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=637.2.)
  Known gap: The three quotes below are all drawn from subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section, § 637.2; they are not independent of one another. Section 637.2(a)'s right of action reaches a violation of "this chapter" as a whole -- the full Invasion of Privacy chapter, §§ 630-638.55 -- not only violations of §§ 631 or 632 specifically; this clause does not restate every other section within that chapter. This clause does not address the statute of limitations applicable to a § 637.2 action, nor § 637.2(d)'s cross-reference preserving Civil Code trade-secret provisions, neither of which was independently verified here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
I, Jordan Lee, acknowledge that I have received and reviewed this document describing California's Invasion of Privacy Act, Penal Code §§ 630-638.55.

Acme, Inc.
